intro: This guide takes your group through “All of Grace (For Teens)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It retells C. H. Spurgeon’s much-loved little book on how a person is saved, freely and entirely by God’s grace, for teens aged about 13 to 18. It suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group, and it serves both teens who are exploring the Christian faith for the first time and those who have grown up in church but have never been sure where they stand with God.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or beforehand at home (8–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own (2–3 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter and its closing “Now — what is this actually about?” section, which puts Spurgeon’s point in plain terms. Spurgeon speaks to the conscience about sin, guilt and judgment, so keep the book’s own emphasis on the free gift in front of everyone. Chapter 8 mentions being tormented by horrible thoughts; if a teen tells you they struggle with intrusive or distressing thoughts, listen kindly and help them find further support from parents, a pastor or a professional. Some teens may want to talk about trusting Jesus for the first time, especially near the end of the book, so leave room to talk privately after a session, and never press anyone to make a decision in front of the group.

weeks.summary: Spurgeon opens with a man whose roadside drinking fountain was criticised by an art critic; he only cared that thousands of thirsty people drank from it, and Spurgeon offers his plain book in the same spirit. He then tells of a poor woman who didn’t answer a minister’s knock because she thought it was the man calling for the rent, when he had come to give her money. Most people hear God the same way, but Spurgeon insists he is “not calling for the rent”: salvation is all of grace, free, and the one knocking is Jesus. The big idea: God’s first word to us is not a demand but an offer.

memory_verse.text: Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.

activity.title: Who’s at the Door?
steps: Retell the story of the woman and the minister, and ask what she missed by staying quiet.
Ask the group to list the things people expect God to “collect” from them when he comes near.
Have each person write privately one honest sentence: “I think what God wants from me is ___.”
Ask them to keep the paper safe and read it again when the group finishes the book.

weeks.summary: Spurgeon builds on Paul’s phrase that God “justifies the ungodly.” Since no one is righteous, Jesus came not to reward good people but to make the guilty right, just as a doctor goes where people are sick and only debtors can have debts cancelled. The gospel is for those who have ignored God and for those who sang in the choir without knowing him; the street-sweeper who arrived washed and in a borrowed suit was sent away because the artist wanted him as he was. The big idea: God’s grace starts where we actually are, so don’t wait to clean yourself up before coming.

memory_verse.text: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness.

activity.title: Come As You Are
steps: Retell the story of the street-sweeper and the artist.
Ask: what are the “borrowed suits” people put on before they come to God, such as acting more spiritual or waiting until they’ve stopped a habit?
Read Spurgeon’s line “The law is for the self-righteous, to humble their pride: the gospel is for the lost, to remove their despair,” and talk about which half people need most.
Invite everyone to pray silently and privately the prayer from the end of the chapter, exactly as they are.

weeks.summary: Only God can justify us, Spurgeon says, because our sin is against him, and when he does, it is settled: “If the Judge acquits me, who can condemn me?” As a guilt-crushed teenager, Spurgeon heard “Look unto me, and be ye saved,” looked, and was justified. But how can a just God let the guilty go? Because the Judge’s own Son took the sentence; the penalty was really paid, and like people leaping into a lifeboat we bring nothing. The big idea: real forgiveness doesn’t pretend sin didn’t matter; Jesus paid its full cost.

memory_verse.text: It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

activity.title: “It’s Fine” or Forgiven?
steps: Ask the group why “it’s fine, whatever” often doesn’t feel like real forgiveness.
List together what the chapter says makes God’s forgiveness different.
Read aloud Spurgeon’s line “God will spare the sinner because He did not spare His Son.”
Encourage everyone to read Luke 23 slowly at home this week, and to stop at the cross and say privately, “He paid it.”

weeks.summary: Some people understand forgiveness but cannot stop sinning, and Spurgeon says salvation must deal with that too: we need to be purified as well as pardoned. God deals with sin’s penalty, its power and one day its presence, and in Ezekiel he promises, “I will give you a new heart.” Like a pig that runs back to the mud however often it is scrubbed, we need a new nature, not just new habits, and the change is God’s work, not ours. The big idea: Christianity is not a self-improvement plan but God giving us a new heart.

memory_verse.text: And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.

activity.title: Hose Down or Make New?
steps: Retell the picture of the cat and the pig, and ask what point Spurgeon is making.
List together the ways people try to “hose themselves down”: new rules, promises, apps, fresh starts.
Talk about why these can help for a while but can’t change a nature.
Ask each person to write privately the one sin they are most tired of losing to, and to pray Ezekiel 36:26 about it each day this week.

weeks.summary: Before he explains faith, Spurgeon points to the source: we are saved by grace, and faith is only the aqueduct that carries the water, not the water itself, so “never make a Christ out of your faith.” A trembling hand can still receive a golden gift. Faith has three parts: knowing who Jesus is and what he did, believing it is true, and trusting, leaning your full weight on him. The big idea: faith isn’t a feeling or a performance; it is resting on Jesus, and what saves is who you lean on, not how hard you lean.

memory_verse.text: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.

activity.title: Know, Believe, Trust
steps: Write the three parts of faith across the top of a sheet: Know, Believe, Trust.
Read John 3:14–18 together and list under “Know” what Jesus says about himself.
Talk about the difference between believing something is true and actually trusting it, using the chair picture from the chapter.
Give a quiet minute for anyone who wishes to tell Jesus privately that they are leaning their whole weight on him.

weeks.summary: Spurgeon gives a run of pictures of faith: the eye that looks, the hand that takes, the mouth that eats, the swimmer who lifts his feet, and the limpet that clings to the rock with no understanding at all. Faith can grow, from clinging, to following a guide, to the trust that comes from love, to obedience, and finally to mature faith like the old woman who wrote “T” and “P” beside the promises she had tried and proved. The big idea: real faith can be small and simple, and it grows as we stop relying on ourselves and lean on Jesus.

memory_verse.text: For we walk by faith, not by sight.

activity.title: Picture Match
activity.materials: Slips of paper with the chapter’s pictures written on them
steps: Write each picture on a slip: eye, hand, mouth, swimmer, limpet, blind man, doctor’s wife, ship’s captain.
In pairs, have teens draw slips and explain what that picture shows about faith.
Ask the group to list ways they already trust people every day, such as a bus driver or a doctor.
Ask each person to write John 6:37 somewhere they will see it this week, ready to mark “T” and “P” beside it when they have seen it hold.

weeks.summary: Spurgeon suggests why God chose faith as the way we receive salvation. Faith simply receives, like a child’s hand taking an apple; it gives all the credit to God; and it connects us to him, as in the story of two men above Niagara Falls, one holding a rope and saved, the other letting go for a bigger log and swept over. Faith is also the mainspring of a holy life, and the key that opens heaven’s gate where pushing fails. The big idea: faith saves not because it is impressive but because it joins us to the One who is.

memory_verse.text: And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.

activity.title: Logs and the Rope
steps: Retell the story of the two men above Niagara Falls.
Ask the group to list the “logs” people cling to in order to feel okay with God.
Talk about why these things are not wrong in themselves but can’t save, because they aren’t tied to the shore.
Have each person make two private lists, “my logs” and “the rope,” and pray silently, letting go of the first and holding on to the second.

weeks.summary: Some people believe everything and still say, “I can do nothing,” but Spurgeon says the gospel begins where we are, like the Good Samaritan who carried the traveller, because Christ died for us when we were without strength. He answers each excuse: I can’t think deeply enough, repent enough, quiet my horrible thoughts, believe, give up my sin, or stand firm with friends. Each time his answer is not “try harder” but that Christ died for people exactly like that, and he points to Luther answering the devil, “Christ died to save sinners.” The big idea: our weakness is not a barrier to grace; it is where grace starts.

memory_verse.text: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.

activity.title: Answer the “I Can’t”
steps: Write each excuse from the chapter on a card: I can’t think, repent, stop these thoughts, believe, give up my sin, stand firm.
Hand them out and have small groups find Spurgeon’s answer to each in the chapter.
Share the answers, and notice together what they all have in common.
Ask each person to write privately the excuse that sounds most like them, with Romans 5:6 underneath, to keep for the week.

weeks.summary: Asked how to get more faith, Spurgeon says the shortest way to believe is to believe, but he also gives practical help: take your puzzles to God, hear the gospel often, and listen to people it has changed, like the man who stepped onto a frozen river only after he saw others cross. Jesus’ invitation gives us the right to come, as John the foreman learned from his employer’s card, and Spurgeon asks why anyone would distrust Jesus. Believing and new birth both come from the same Lord, and we trust a living Saviour who is our Advocate. The big idea: faith grows by looking at Jesus and the evidence, not by staring at our faith.

memory_verse.text: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.

activity.title: Your Name on the Card
steps: Retell the story of John the foreman and his employer’s card.
Read Matthew 11:28 aloud and ask the group what it means to treat it as an invitation with your name on it.
Have each person write Matthew 11:28 on a card to keep, with their own name at the top.
Encourage everyone to ask a Christian they respect this week to tell them in ten minutes how they came to trust Jesus.

weeks.summary: Peter says Jesus, exalted to God’s right hand, gives both repentance and forgiveness, and Spurgeon says they always go together: forgiveness without a change of heart would be a licence to sin. Repentance is not the cause of forgiveness but its companion, “a heart broken for sin, and from sin,” and a lifelong grace. It comes from Jesus too, through events like a crowing rooster or an earthquake, and it is not pumped up from our own dry well but given as we look at him. The big idea: repentance is not earning forgiveness; it is turning around because we have been loved.

memory_verse.text: God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins.

activity.title: What Turning Looks Like
steps: Read Luke 22:54–62 together, noticing the moment “the Lord turned and looked at Peter.”
Ask the group to describe two wrong ideas the chapter rejects: feeling bad long enough to earn forgiveness, and forgiveness that never changes you.
List together what real repentance often looks like in everyday life, using the chapter’s examples.
Ask each person to write privately one thing they sense God asking them to turn from, and one concrete step they will take this week.

weeks.summary: Many new believers fear they will fall away, and Spurgeon warns that those who trust Jesus to start them but themselves to keep them will not hold on. Living faith needs fresh grace daily, the road has its Hill of Difficulty and Valley of Humiliation, and God’s promise to keep us shows we will need keeping. But God is faithful: he strengthens what he starts, keeps us holy as well as safe, and has called us into partnership with his Son, so “unless Jesus sinks, the believer will never drown.” The big idea: we don’t keep ourselves saved; God keeps us, and that is why we keep going.

memory_verse.text: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

activity.title: In the Same Boat
steps: Read Spurgeon’s line “If you look to Christ for your beginnings, beware of looking to yourself for your endings,” and ask what it means.
List together the things that make teens afraid they will drift from God.
Talk about why the chapter says God’s faithfulness, not ours, is the answer, and why that is not an excuse for careless living.
Ask each person to write privately the fear that most worries them, with “God is faithful” written underneath, and to pray about it each night this week.

weeks.summary: Spurgeon ends by speaking straight to the reader: reading about grace is pointless unless you take hold of it, like seeing food in a shop and staying hungry. He tells how he stopped writing at that page to kneel and pray for the reader, urges anyone who trusts Jesus to live from free grace, which guards against both pride and despair, and to tell others, starting at home. His last words plead, “Let it be NOW,” and invite the reader to meet him in heaven. The big idea: grace is something to receive today and then live from, gratefully, for the rest of life.

memory_verse.text: Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

activity.title: Back to the Door
activity.materials: The sentences written in week 1, and paper and pens
steps: Ask everyone to read privately the sentence they wrote in the first week about what God wants from them.
Ask: has the book changed how you hear God’s knock? Let anyone who wants to share do so.
Read Spurgeon’s words about pride and despair, and talk about what a life shaped by grace looks like.
Invite each person to decide privately on one step this week: either to trust Jesus today, or to tell one person what grace has meant to them.
Let the group know you are glad to talk with anyone privately after the session.
